e.t: Abenezer is a proper name, also rendered Avenezer. It identifies a named place or designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object in general. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, both times in 1 Samuel: 4:1 and 7:12. The available references establish where the name appears, while the name itself does not provide enough information here to explain the particular significance of either passage.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “purify”: to make a person or thing clean and ready for a proper use or approach to God. It describes an action of cleansing rather than merely labeling something as clean. The word occurs 31 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages involving people preparing themselves, being cleansed, or being set apart for sacred responsibilities. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being purified and the surrounding instruction, but its central idea remains cleansing for fitness or holy use.

This Greek word means “street” or “highway,” referring to a route where people travel. It is a noun for a public way or roadway rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament collection represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 3 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: a street, road, or highway used for movement through or between places.

Adōraim, also rendered Athorem, is a proper name referring to a place or location. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Chronicles 11:9. Because a proper name identifies rather than describes an action, quality, or concept, its basic meaning is the name itself rather than a broader idea. The surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain the place’s role in that particular account.

Aizel, also rendered Ezil, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 10:27. The available lexical information identifies it as a proper name, so its meaning is primarily the individual it names, not a general concept that can be translated into an English definition. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the person’s place in that passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “goat,” referring to the animal. It is used throughout the Old Testament Greek corpus for goats as ordinary animals, including those involved in herds, offerings, and other everyday references. The word occurs 74 times in 74 verses, from Genesis through Song of Songs, so its basic meaning remains consistent across a broad range of passages. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but the word itself identifies a goat or goats. [Evidence: identity; occurrences.]

This Greek LXX adjective describes something done “unwillingly”—without a person’s willing agreement. It focuses on the manner of an action, showing that someone acts without desire or consent rather than freely choosing to do so. The word occurs twice in the LXX corpus, once in Job 14:17 and once in 4 Maccabees 11:12. The surrounding verse determines the specific situation, but the word itself consistently points to unwilling action.

This Greek LXX noun refers to marks or targets—the points set out for aiming or directing something. Its basic sense is concrete and visual: it identifies a designated point rather than an action or quality. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at 1 Samuel 20:20. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain how the word functions in that particular passage.

ἀμφίασις refers to a garment or clothing—the covering worn on the body. It is a noun naming apparel rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs three times, all in Job, so its basic sense is consistent, while its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding wording. English renderings record “clothing,” which matches the central meaning. The word itself does not identify a particular type, material, or symbolic use of garment.

This LXX verb means “renew”: to make something new again or restore it to renewed condition. It can describe renewal involving a person, a people, or what has become weakened or worn. The word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, including three times in Psalms, but its central sense remains the same—bringing renewed life or condition. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “rip up”—to tear something apart or pull it up forcefully. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament material represented here, at Amos 1:13. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, the specific object being torn up and the full force of the action must be understood from that passage itself. Its basic meaning remains the forceful tearing or pulling up of something.

This Greek LXX verb means “set up against,” describing the act of taking a position in opposition to someone or something. It is an action word rather than a name or description. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Baruch 3:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is opposition or standing against. [Evidence: p03:word:lxx:L701214:identity; p03:word:lxx:L701214:occurrences; p01:word:lxx:L701214:reference:0]

This noun means “opposition” or “hostility”—active resistance or antagonism directed against someone or something. It describes a condition of being set against another rather than agreement or cooperation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 3:13. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning points to antagonism, resistance, or hostile opposition.

Arbēlos, also called Arvilos, is a proper name. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 9:2. The lexical information identifies the name but does not describe its location, history, or role. Its precise significance in that passage must therefore come from the surrounding verse and narrative. The name itself is not presented as a general quality, action, or theological concept.

Ariōrgim, also rendered Arioryim, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or named figure in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the LXX, at 2 Samuel 21:19. Without the surrounding verse text, no further description of the person or the name’s specific role can be stated responsibly. Its meaning, therefore, is its function as a personal name in that passage.

Asemona is a proper name, rendered “Asemona,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times: twice in Numbers and once in Joshua. Its use is therefore tied to identifying a named place or location in the biblical text, while its name itself is not translated into a separate concept. The form is also presented as “Asemōna,” reflecting the same name in English rendering.

This verb means “supply with necessaries”: it describes the action of providing what is needed. As a verb, it presents this provision as something done for another person or group, rather than naming a thing or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 32:10. Its precise force in that verse must be read from the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is the act of supplying necessities.

This adjective describes someone or something as “voiceless” or “dumb”—without a speaking voice or unable to speak. It can refer to literal silence or speechlessness, while the surrounding passage determines the precise situation. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: once in Isaiah and twice in the deuterocanonical books Wisdom and 2 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains focused on the absence of voice or spoken expression.

Aōdas, also rendered Aothas, is a proper name—the personal name of an individual rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:6. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s identity and role in that genealogy cannot be explained further from this entry alone.

Belaan, also rendered Velaan, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 15:27. The available meaning is therefore the name itself; the supplied information does not establish a separate definition or broader lexical use. Its precise identity and role belong to the surrounding passage, but this entry should be understood as a personal or place name, not as a common noun or theological concept.

This word means “library”. It is a noun for a place where books or written materials are kept. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it appears three times, including passages in Ezra, Esther, and 2 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on a collection or repository of written works, while the surrounding passage determines how that place functions in a particular verse.

Gug is a proper name, referring to a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The Greek Old Testament form is rendered “Gug,” while the lexical definition also gives “Goug.” It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 5:4. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name’s specific role in that verse cannot be described further; its basic meaning is the personal name itself.

This verb means “train”: to prepare or strengthen someone through practice. It describes purposeful development rather than a single accidental action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 10:15. The surrounding verse text is not available, so the particular force of the word there cannot be described more narrowly. Its basic sense remains active preparation through training or exercise.

This verb means “nod,” describing a movement of the head used to signal or communicate something. It refers to a physical gesture rather than a spoken statement. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Psalms and once in Sirach. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation, but its basic meaning remains the act of nodding. It is distinct from words that describe speaking, pointing, or other bodily movements.

This verb means to travel through or pass through a place. It describes movement along or across an area, rather than simply being present there. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 41 times, showing a recurring word for journeying through a location. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what place or route the surrounding passage describes. The word is used in the Greek translation of the Old Testament and related writings, not as a Greek New Testament entity.

This noun refers to a whirlpool or eddy—a circular, twisting movement of water. It describes water caught in a powerful swirling motion rather than flowing in a straight course. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Job 37:9. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to a concentrated, revolving current of water. It is a vivid term for turbulent water that turns and draws movement inward.

This noun means “runner”—a person who runs or moves swiftly. It presents running as the defining activity or role of the person described, without by itself specifying why he runs or what happens around him. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times across four verses, including passages in Job, Proverbs, and Amos. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX verb means “sprout out”: to emerge and begin growing like a plant from the ground or a stem. It describes visible new growth, whether a branch, shoot, or vegetation appearing. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in Numbers, Job, and Isaiah. Its central picture is something living coming forth and developing, so the surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis is on the act of emerging or on the resulting growth.

This LXX verb means “shake off”: to dislodge or cast something away by shaking. It describes a deliberate action rather than simply moving or trembling. The word occurs 21 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, including passages from Exodus, Judges, Nehemiah, Psalms, Isaiah, and other books. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being shaken off and the surrounding sentence.

This verb means to divert or avoid—to turn something aside or keep away from it. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its exact force depends on what is being diverted or avoided in the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Amos 5:8. The word’s basic sense remains focused and practical: changing direction or deliberately steering clear of something. The surrounding verse is needed to explain its particular force there.

This word is a proper name, given in the lexical definition as “Elbōydad” or “Elvuthath.” It identifies a named individual or place rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In this LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Joshua 15:30. The available record does not provide surrounding verse text, so its specific referent must be determined from that passage.

This Greek LXX word means “in.” It is used as a preposition or adverb to indicate that someone or something is located within a place, setting, circumstance, or sphere. In English, it commonly introduces the surrounding situation in which an action or condition exists. It is very common in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, occurring 12,728 times, so its precise force in a particular sentence depends on the surrounding words.

This noun refers to the fourth stomach of a ruminating animal, such as cattle, sheep, or goats. Ruminating animals have a digestive system with several stomach compartments, and this word identifies the final one. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 18:3. Its meaning is specific and bodily rather than symbolic in the lexical information available here; the surrounding verse would be needed to explain how the term functions in that passage.

This verb means to swear in excuse—to use an oath as a defense or justification. It describes speech in which a person appeals to a solemn promise while explaining or defending conduct. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, all in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in each passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains an oath offered as an excuse or defense.

This verb means “perjure”: to make a false statement under oath or violate a sworn promise. It describes deliberate untruthfulness connected with an oath, rather than ordinary mistaken speech. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Wisdom 14:28. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the breaking or betraying of a sworn commitment.

This Greek LXX verb means “pour on”: to cause a liquid or other substance to flow over or onto something. It describes an action rather than a thing, so its exact object is supplied by the sentence where it appears. The word occurs 22 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, including instructions connected with offerings and acts of pouring. Its central idea remains the deliberate placing or flowing of something onto a surface or object.

Eromaph is a proper name, referring to a particular person named in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general term describing an action, quality, or spiritual idea. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Nehemiah 3:10, and its normal meaning is simply the personal designation Eromaph. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain that person’s specific role in the passage, but the name itself does not provide further meaning.

This adjective means “well-rounded” or “round,” describing something with a rounded, complete shape. It is a descriptive word rather than an action or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Wisdom 5:21. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise reference in that passage cannot be explained further; its established meaning remains the description of something rounded in form.

This verb means to seduce someone to sin—to lead a person toward wrongdoing. It describes an active influence that draws another person into sinful action, rather than merely describing sin itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 39:35. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is clear: persuading or enticing someone into sin.

Zechri is a proper name referring to a person, also rendered Zekhri. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or object, so its ordinary meaning is its identifying name rather than a broader concept. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times across nine verses, appearing in Exodus, 1 Chronicles, and Nehemiah. The precise person identified depends on the surrounding passage and genealogy in each occurrence.

Zorobabel is a proper name, also rendered Zorovavel. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs 23 times, especially in Haggai, Ezra, Zechariah, and Nehemiah. The name appears in accounts and genealogical records connected with Israel’s restoration after exile, but its precise significance in any particular verse depends on that passage’s context.

Ēmath, also rendered Imath, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. It functions as the name of a particular place or region in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs 13 times in 11 Old Testament verses, from 2 Samuel 8:9 through Ezekiel 48:1. Its exact significance in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the word itself identifies Ēmath or Imath. [p03:word:lxx:L705980:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L705980:occurrences]

Thaiman, also rendered Theman, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books. It identifies a named person or place according to the surrounding passage, rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. The name occurs 24 times in this Greek LXX corpus, from Genesis through Baruch. Its exact reference may therefore vary by passage, but its basic meaning remains the identifying name “Thaiman” or “Theman.”

Iethraam is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It appears once in the LXX, at 1 Chronicles 3:3. The name itself is presented as “Iethraam,” without an additional definition or descriptive meaning. Because no verse text or wider context is included here, the word is best understood simply as the personal name it records, rather than as a common noun or an idea that describes an action, quality, or object.

Ierimoth is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears six times in six verses, five times in 1 Chronicles and once in 2 Chronicles. Because it is a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it distinguishes one person from others in the genealogical, musical, administrative, and priestly records where it occurs. The name is rendered as “Ierimōth” or “Ierimoth.”

This word is a proper name, identifying a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. It is given as “Ioudias; Iuthias,” two forms associated with the same name. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 26:31. The name’s precise identification and significance depend on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included in this word-level record.

Iōanan, also written Ioanan, is a personal name used for people in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, object, or spiritual concept. The name occurs 30 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing across historical and prophetic books. Its precise reference changes from passage to passage because different people may bear the same name; the surrounding verse identifies which person is meant.

Iona is a proper name, rendered “Iōna” or “Iona.” It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament text, but the available information does not establish which in each occurrence. This name appears three times in the Greek Old Testament: once in 2 Kings and twice in Jonah. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding verse context.

This verb means to sleep or to be asleep. It describes the ordinary state of resting during sleep and can refer either to the act of sleeping or to someone who is already asleep. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 29 times, chiefly in Old Testament books, with one occurrence in the deuterocanonical writings. Its use across narrative and wisdom writings shows a normal word for physical sleep, while the precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “bear fruit,” describing the production of fruit or a fruitful result. It presents fruit-bearing as an action rather than merely naming fruit itself. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Leviticus, Deuteronomy, and Daniel. Its exact sense in any one passage depends on what is being described, but its central idea remains producing or yielding fruit. [Evidence: p03:word:lxx:L707173:identity; p03:word:lxx:L707173:occurrences]

This verb means “receive; admit”: to accept or take something in. As a verb, it describes an action of accepting rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs twice, once in Exodus and once in Deuteronomy. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains receiving or admitting what is presented.

This noun means “catapult,” a machine used to hurl objects toward a target. It refers to a weapon or siege device rather than to an action or personal quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs five times, all in 4 Maccabees. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its particular use in any one passage, but the word’s ordinary meaning is a catapult.

This word is a proper name rendered “Kedrōn” or “Kethron.” It identifies a named biblical referent rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 17 times across 15 verses, from Judges through 1 Maccabees. The name itself is not given a further definition here, so its precise significance in any particular passage comes from that passage’s surrounding text.

Kenezi is a proper name preserved as “Kenezi.” It identifies a particular person, family, or place in the Old Testament Greek translation, but the available wording does not specify which in every occurrence. The name appears three times in the Greek Old Testament, across three verses. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding passage, since a proper name identifies rather than describes someone or something.

This word means “pupil,” referring to the dark, central opening of the eye. It is a noun used for a specific part of the eye rather than for a person or general sight. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs eight times, including passages from Deuteronomy, Psalms, Proverbs, Zechariah, Sirach, and other books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains the eye’s pupil.

This Greek LXX noun means “dominion”: the power, authority, or ruling strength by which someone governs or prevails. It can describe dominion as an active force rather than merely a position or title. The word appears 30 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, including passages in Genesis, Judges, Job, and the Psalms. Its exact force in any verse is clarified by the surrounding sentence and subject.

This noun means “wave,” a moving rise or swell of water. It can refer to one wave or to waves as a group, describing water in motion. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 24 times, including passages in Exodus, Job, and the Psalms. The word’s basic sense remains a physical movement of water; the surrounding verse determines whether it is being used simply as a description or within a broader comparison.

This Greek LXX adverb means “secretly”: doing something without others knowing or without openly revealing it. It describes the manner of an action rather than naming a person, object, or event. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in the Old Testament and once in the Deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains concealed or unannounced action.

This verb means “turn into stone” or “petrify.” It describes making something stone-like or causing it to become stone. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, in Exodus 35:33. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning centers on transformation into stone. This is a Greek LXX word, so its meaning is presented within that Greek Old Testament setting.

Marma is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 8:10, and its role there is simply to identify a person. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, no further claim about Marma’s family connection or historical significance can be made from the name alone.

Massēpha, also rendered Massifa, is a proper name for a place rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies locations mentioned in accounts from Joshua, Judges, Jeremiah, and 1 Maccabees. The name occurs 22 times across 21 verses in this Greek Old Testament corpus. Because it is a place name, its precise significance in any particular passage depends on which location called Massēpha is being mentioned.

This word means “hate” or “hatred,” describing strong hostility or aversion toward someone or something. It functions as a noun, naming that hostile feeling, and can also describe what is characterized by hatred. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 11 times across 10 verses, including passages in 2 Samuel, Esther, Psalms, Ecclesiastes, and Jeremiah. Its repeated rendering as “hatred” confirms that the central idea is an intense opposing feeling, rather than a momentary dislike.

Moore is a proper name, used to identify a particular person, place, or other named entity rather than to describe a general idea or action. In the Greek LXX corpus, this name occurs once, at 2 Samuel 23:28. The meaning is simply “Moore”; without the verse text and surrounding context, the exact referent cannot be identified more precisely. Its role is therefore best understood as a specific name whose referent is determined by the passage.

This adjective describes someone or something involved in “slaying children” or “killing children.” It identifies the destructive act of killing young children rather than naming a person, place, or object by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Wisdom 11:7. The precise force of the adjective in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the killing of children.

This Greek LXX verb means “make of wood,” describing the act of producing or constructing something from timber. It is a practical action word rather than a name for the wooden object itself. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in passages from 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any one passage depends on what is being made and the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains the making or forming of something with wood.

This adverb describes something done openly and willingly—that is, plainly and by choice rather than secretly or under compulsion. It expresses the manner in which an action or statement is carried out. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Hosea 14:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains an action performed openly and with willingness.

This noun means “sharpness” or “pointedness”—the quality of being sharp, having a keen edge, or coming to a point. It describes a physical or figurative quality rather than an action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 8:16. The surrounding verse is needed to determine how this basic idea functions there, but the word itself centers on keenness, sharp edges, or a pointed quality.

This Greek LXX noun means a mountain or mount—a raised area of land, whether viewed as part of the landscape or identified as a particular height. It is used throughout the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings for physical mountains and named or recognizable mountainous places. The word occurs 185 times in this LXX corpus, so it is a broad, ordinary landscape term rather than a rare or specialized expression. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding context.

This word means “not.” It is an adverb used to deny, reject, or negate what is being said or described. In the Greek Old Testament, it commonly marks something as not happening, not being true, or not belonging to someone or something. It occurs 2,646 times in the LXX, so its basic force is broad and consistent across many kinds of sentences. Its precise emphasis depends on the words and statement surrounding it.

This noun means “Passover,” the name used for the Passover observance in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies the subject or occasion being referred to rather than describing an action or quality. The word occurs 29 times across 28 Old Testament verses in this Greek corpus, beginning in Exodus and continuing through Ezekiel. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and wording.

This Greek LXX adjective means “on foot,” describing someone who travels or proceeds by walking rather than by riding or using a vehicle. It is a concise way to describe a person’s manner of movement. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 15:17. The word itself gives the manner of travel, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular situation in which it is used. Its basic sense remains straightforward: movement made by walking.

This adverb means “notably” or “manifestly,” describing something presented as especially clear, evident, or conspicuous. It tells the reader how an action, statement, or condition is expressed rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 8:2. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its basic sense emphasizes something made plainly noticeable or clearly apparent.

This word means “senior” or “older.” It can describe someone who is advanced in age, or function as a noun for an older or senior person. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 186 times, showing that it is a regularly used term for age or seniority rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on whether it describes a person or stands for one. The word appears from Genesis through Susanna.

This adjective describes something that is acceptable or pleasing to the one receiving or evaluating it. It can refer to a person, action, or offering that is regarded favorably rather than rejected. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word occurs three times, in Proverbs and Wisdom. Its precise emphasis in any sentence depends on what is being described and whose approval is in view, but its central idea remains being acceptable or welcome. [Actually, the word appears in Proverbs 11:20, Proverbs 16:15, and Wisdom 9:12.]

This noun means an “offence” or “provocation”—something regarded as offensive or provocative. It names the matter that causes offence or stirs opposition, rather than describing a person or action by itself. The word appears nine times in the LXX corpus, in books ranging from Deuteronomy through later Jewish writings. Its basic sense remains focused on what is viewed as an offence or provocation.

This word means “wheat,” the grain produced by a wheat plant. It is a noun naming the crop or its harvested grain, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 147 times, showing that it is a familiar agricultural term across this corpus. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the grain itself.

This word is a proper name: “Ramōth,” also rendered “Rhamoth.” It identifies a named person or place rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 13 times across 13 verses, beginning in Deuteronomy and continuing through Ezekiel. Its exact referent in any particular passage must be determined from that passage’s surrounding text.

This adjective means “filthy,” describing something dirty or unclean. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Zechariah 3:3–4. Its basic function is to identify a condition of uncleanness, whether referring to something that needs cleansing or to a person associated with such a condition. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the specific force of the word in each occurrence.

Samaia is a personal name, also rendered Samea. It identifies people in the Greek Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. The name occurs 17 times across 16 verses in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in genealogical, family, priestly, and historical lists or accounts. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is primarily the person it identifies in each passage; the surrounding verse is needed to distinguish which Samaia is intended. It appears from 2 Samuel through Nehemiah.

Satan is the name of a personal spiritual adversary. As a proper name in the Greek Old Testament, it identifies Satan rather than describing an ordinary object, action, or quality. This word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both occurrences appearing in 1 Kings 11:14. The name itself gives the person’s identity, while the surrounding passage is needed to understand the particular role or action associated with him there. In this corpus, the word has a direct and specific meaning: Satan.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Sēdanin” or “Sithanin,” rather than a common term describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is therefore its identification of a named person, group, or place; the available information does not specify which. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Ezra 3:7. The surrounding verse text would be needed to determine exactly whom or what the name identifies there.

This adjective means “of baking,” describing something connected with the work or activity of baking. It functions as a descriptive word rather than naming an action by itself. In the LXX, it occurs once, in Genesis 40:17, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided here. Its precise role in that verse depends on the noun it describes and the immediate context.

This Greek LXX noun means “grain,” referring to the seed or harvested food produced from it.
